analysis.one_liner: Taxes executives who sell option stock faster than their own employees' 401(k) rules allow and forces disclosure of retired-executive perks.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to House Ways and Means the day it was introduced on September 24, 2002, and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, written after the Enron and WorldCom collapses, would have made corporate executives play by the same rules as their employees. Executives would pay a 50 percent extra tax if they sold company stock from exercised options faster than the rules of their company's own 401(k) plan allow. Shareholders would get to see and vote on perks given to retired executives — company planes, club memberships, homes — or the company would pay a 50 percent tax on them. And executives' set-aside deferred pay would be taxed unless it stayed reachable by the company's creditors, so executives could no longer be first in line ahead of employees when a company goes bankrupt.
analysis.who_benefits: Rank-and-file employees with company stock in their 401(k) plans, whose holding rules executives would have to live under too, and whose own retirement savings would no longer sit behind secured executive compensation if a company collapses. Shareholders would also gain the right to see and vote on retired-executive perks before they are paid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees with company stock in 401(k) plans

how_it_helps.text: Executives would face a 50 percent additional tax on any 'disqualified disposition' — selling stock acquired by exercising options in a way that would violate the sale restrictions in their own company's 401(k) plan — putting insiders under the same lockup rules their employees already live under [S2][S3].

Shareholders would gain visibility and control over retirement perks: a company would pay a 50 percent tax on the net cost of perks given to retired executives (corporate planes, apartments, club memberships, event tickets, personal services) unless the perk contract was disclosed to shareholders and approved by a majority in a separate vote [S3].

Deferred compensation that is set aside in a funded trust would be taxed when no longer at risk, unless the executive's rights stay no greater than a general creditor's — a direct response to arrangements that let executives keep their deferred pay while rank-and-file employees lost retirement savings in bankruptcies like Enron's [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporate insiders at publicly traded companies, who would face a 50 percent additional tax on selling option stock faster than their company's own 401(k) plan allows, a 50 percent tax on a company's cost of perks given to retired executives (unless shareholders approve the perks in a separate vote), and immediate taxation of funded deferred compensation. Their corporations would bear the perk tax and new compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate insiders and publicly traded corporations

drawbacks.text: The 50 percent additional tax on disqualified dispositions is a blunt instrument: it applies whenever a sale would violate the company's own 401(k) plan restrictions, and if a company has multiple plans the most restrictive provision governs, which could sweep in routine sales by insiders subject to ordinary blackout or lockup windows [S3].

The perk tax reaches the corporation, not just the executive, so companies and ultimately their shareholders would bear the cost of perks given before shareholder-approval rules kick in — existing contracts get a grace period until the first annual shareholder meeting after enactment [S3].

Defining 'funded deferred compensation' and 'corporate insider' turns on detailed legal tests (Sections 16(a) and 12 of the Securities Exchange Act, creditor-reachability of trusts), which would generate complicated compliance questions for companies and their advisers [S3].

Retired-executive perks could still be provided tax-free if disclosed and approved by a shareholder majority, so the disclosure-and-vote path leaves room for perks to continue where shareholders do not object [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for ordinary people are real but modest in scope: employees would gain the guarantee that executives face the same stock-holding restrictions they do, shareholders could see and vote on retired-executive perks, and executives' deferred pay could no longer be structured to outrank everyone else's claims in a bankruptcy. The costs fall on executives and corporations — a 50 percent tax on fast option sales, on undisclosed perks, and on funded deferred comp — which is the point of the bill, though some of that cost could pass through to companies' compliance budgets and, at the margin, compensation design. The main design risk is over-breadth: tying the option-stock rule to whatever restrictions exist in a company's 401(k) plan, and applying the strictest one across multiple plans, could tax insider sales that carry no abuse. On balance the bill targets executive self-dealing directly and its costs land mainly on the people it targets, with a real but debatable complexity cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the tax-writing committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in early January 2003.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 24, 2002, roughly ten months into the corporate scandal wave that had begun with Enron's December 2001 collapse, and was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax law [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, and no vote are recorded before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].
The bill's sponsor and all cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Ways and Means Committee was controlled by Republicans [S3][S4].

Congress did pass some corporate accountability legislation in this period, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of July 2002, but the executive-pay and retirement-parity tax rules in this bill were not among them [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate insiders are better off because the bill died: quick sales of option stock, undisclosed retirement perks, and secured deferred compensation all remain untaxed as before. The Ways and Means Committee majority that never scheduled the bill also avoided a vote on a post-scandal executive-pay measure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Executives keeping quick option sales and perks tax-free

industries.industry: Corporate executives and insiders at publicly traded companies
industries.note: The bill would hit corporate insiders with a 50 percent additional tax on quick sales of option stock, on the net cost of perks given to retired executives, and on funded deferred compensation. Their ability to cash out options immediately, collect perks quietly, and hold secured deferred pay ahead of creditors is exactly what the bill targets.

Publicly traded corporations would owe a 50 percent tax on the net cost of perks provided to retired executives unless shareholders approved the perk contracts in a separate vote. Companies would also face new compliance and disclosure obligations, and compensation design would have to shift away from funded deferred comp plans.
